product.title: Japanese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Ten Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Japanese: every Japanese character has its rōmaji reading printed right above it, with short dialogues, word-for-word translations, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Japanese is far more learnable than its reputation suggests: verbs never change for the person, there are no articles and no plurals to juggle, and hundreds of loanwords come straight from English. Complete with hiragana and katakana tables, summaries of particles, verb forms and counters, basic kanji, and an English–Japanese glossary.

blocks.text: Japanese has a fearsome reputation, and most of it is misplaced. What makes people give up isn't the grammar — Japanese grammar is actually tidy and predictable — but the three writing systems blocking the way on page one. Before learning a single sentence, learners are told to memorize 92 letters.

This course refuses that order. Every Japanese character in it comes with **its rōmaji reading printed right above it**, just like the furigana in Japanese children's books. That means you can start reading real sentences in the first minute, while the characters stick on their own through repetition — not through memorizing tables.

It's built around conversations you can use straight away: introducing yourself, asking prices, telling the time, inviting people, and then telling what happened yesterday. The grammar explanations are deliberately short. What's long isn't the theory but the practice.

Its ten units cover the whole of **Level A1 (CEFR)**, roughly equivalent to **JLPT N5** in Japan: about 600 words, 80-odd basic kanji, and all the core sentence patterns — です, ます, particles, adjectives, the past tense, and the て-form.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20–30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours broken into pieces. Language sticks through short, frequent repetition.
Read aloud. Japanese is pronounced very regularly — once your ear knows the sounds, your eyes stop needing the rōmaji.

Don't try to memorize the hiragana table completely first. The tables on the following pages are for reference, not a gate. The characters you meet again and again in sentences will stick by themselves.
Keep a small notebook. Copying Japanese characters by hand is the fastest way to remember them.

blocks.text: One thing no book can replace: someone to talk to. Use this course to prepare the material, then look for chances to use it with real people.
Enjoy learning. *[がんばって|Ganbatte]！*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones set up.

blocks.text: This course is designed for **self-study**. Each unit is meant to be finished in one or two sittings of about 30 minutes. What matters isn't how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Readings above the characters
This is the format you'll see throughout the course:

blocks.title: Example
items: [わたし|watashi]は[インドネシアじん|Indoneshia-jin]です。
I'm from Indonesia.
*literally: I — as-for — Indonesia-person — am.*

blocks.text: The small colored letters above the characters are **rōmaji**, the way to sound out the characters in the Latin alphabet. Read the Japanese first; only glance up when you get stuck. Over time your eyes stop going up there — and that's the sign you can read.
How each unit is organized
Every unit has the same structure, and the order is deliberate:

items: **会話 Kaiwa (dialogue)** — first read the Japanese aloud without looking at the meaning. Let your ear work before your brain demands an explanation. Each unit has two dialogues.

**Word-for-word translation** — the small italic line under the meaning. This is the part people skip most, yet it's where you see how Japanese *thinks*. Example: [わたし|watashi]は[がくせい|gakusei]です literally means “I — as-for — student — am”, not “I am a student”.
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange.
**Grammar boxes** — one sentence pattern, explained once, with its table.
**Vocabulary in this unit** — the unit's new words: the characters, the reading in kana and rōmaji, and the meaning.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've really tried.

blocks.title: You can do the exercises on screen
items: If you open this course through the Linguo dashboard, every Exercises page has a button that turns the questions into interactive practice: build sentences by tapping word tiles, fill in the blanks by typing, and get your answers checked instantly.
Marking is deliberately lenient — capitalization and punctuation are ignored. For free translation questions you can mark your own answer as correct too.

blocks.text: Wave review

At the end of each unit there's a **Wave review** line: a short instruction to go back to an earlier unit. It isn't decoration: languages fade because they aren't revisited, not because they weren't studied deeply enough. Five minutes rereading an old dialogue does more than thirty minutes memorizing new words.

blocks.title: If you only have 15 minutes today
items: Reread yesterday's unit dialogue aloud (5 minutes).
Do just one exercise from that unit (5 minutes).
Read the first dialogue of the next unit without looking at the meaning (5 minutes).
That counts as a full day of study. This course is designed so that busy days don't break the chain.

blocks.text: Japanese is written with three systems at once, in the same sentence. It sounds excessive, but each system has a different job — and once the jobs are clear, the mix actually helps your eye separate the words.

head: Script
Example
Its job
rows: Native Japanese words and all the grammatical bits: particles, verb endings, adjectives. It's the most frequent, and the most important to recognize.
Loanwords from foreign languages, names of foreign countries and people, brand names, and sound effects. The shapes are more angular.
Characters of Chinese origin that stand for meaning, not sound. Used for the roots of nouns, verbs, and adjectives. One kanji can have several readings.

blocks.text: An ordinary sentence uses all three at once:

blocks.title: One sentence, three scripts
items: [わたし|watashi]は[インドネシア|Indoneshia]の[学生|gakusei]です。
I'm a student from Indonesia.
わたし・は・の・です = hiragana · インドネシア = katakana · 学生 = kanji.

blocks.text: **Rōmaji** (ローマ字) — the Latin alphabet — isn't a fourth script but a support. In Japan, rōmaji appears only on station signs and passports. In this course it sits above the characters as a temporary crutch, not as something for you to copy.

blocks.title: Suggested order
items: **Weeks 1–2:** get to know hiragana while working through Units 1–3. Don't memorize the table all at once.
**Weeks 3–4:** get to know katakana. It appears less often, but once you can read it, hundreds of loanwords become readable without memorizing — サッカー sakkā = soccer.
**After that:** kanji, little by little. A list of 80 basic kanji is at the back of the course. There's no point chasing kanji before your sentences flow.

blocks.text: Writing has rules too: strokes go **left to right, top to bottom**, and horizontal lines usually come before vertical ones. If the order is right, Japanese people can read your handwriting even when the shapes aren't neat yet.

Good news for English speakers: Japanese has **very few sounds that will be new** to your mouth. There are just five vowels — a as in *father*, i as in *machine*, u as in *put* (lips unrounded), e as in *bed*, o as in *go* but shorter — and they're always short and crisp, never gliding into “ay” or “ow” as English vowels do.
Syllables, not letters

Japanese isn't built from letters but from **syllables of equal length**. か = ka, き = ki. Each syllable counts as one beat, and the beats are even — which is why Japanese sounds like dripping water rather than waves.

head: Point
Example
Explanation
rows: Length **changes the meaning**: おばあさん = grandmother, おばさん = aunt. Written by adding a vowel (ああ), or with the ー mark in katakana.
A small つ (っ) means a one-beat pause before the next consonant. きって = stamp, きて = come.
ん counts as a full beat, not the tail of the previous letter: ni-ho-n, three beats.
The u at the end of a word is barely voiced: dess, not de-su. Likewise し in ました → mash-ta.
Somewhere between r and l, with the tip of the tongue tapping the roof of the mouth once — like the quick “tt” in American *butter* or *water*.
Not the English f with teeth on the lip; the lips barely come together, like gently blowing out a candle.

blocks.text: Pitch accent

Japanese has no heavy stress like English, but it does have **high and low pitch**. はし can mean bridge or chopsticks depending on pitch. At A1 you don't need to chase this — context almost always saves you. What matters more is keeping every syllable the same length.

blocks.title: The three most common pronunciation mistakes
items: **Stretching vowels at random.** ありがとう isn't a-ri-ga-tooo; the length is exactly two beats on とう.
**Saying the final u too clearly.** です is *dess*, ます is *mass*. This is the difference between sounding natural and sounding like you're reading a table.
**Stressing syllables the English way.** English speakers punch one syllable and swallow the rest (*a-ri-GA-to*). In Japanese, the beats are even.

blocks.text: This is reference, not homework. Come back to this page whenever you meet a character in a unit that you don't recognize. Hiragana is read **row by row, left to right**: a-i-u-e-o, ka-ki-ku-ke-ko, and so on. This is the order Japanese dictionaries use, so learning it pays off twice.
Gojūon — the 46 basic characters

Note three sounds that break the pattern: **し** is *shi* (not si), **ち** is *chi* (not ti), **つ** is *tsu* (not tu). And **を** — although it sits in the w row of the table — is read *o*; it's used only as the object particle, never inside a word.
Dakuten and handakuten — voiced sounds
Two small strokes at the top right (゛) turn an unvoiced consonant into a voiced one: か ka → が ga. A small circle (゜) is used only on the h row, turning it into p: は ha → ぱ pa.
Yōon — gliding sounds
A small や・ゆ・よ written after a character from the i column merges the two into **one beat**: き + ゃ = きゃ *kya*, one beat, not two.

blocks.title: Three characters that behave oddly
items: **は** is read *wa* when used as a particle: わたし**は** = watashi **wa**. Inside ordinary words it stays *ha*.
**へ** is read *e* when used as the direction particle: とうきょう**へ** = Tōkyō **e**.
**を** is always read *o*, and only appears as the object particle.

blocks.text: Katakana spells exactly the same sounds as hiragana — ア and あ are both *a*. Only the job is different: katakana is used for loanwords, foreign names, brand names, and sound effects. The shapes are more angular, with fewer curves.
Gojūon — the 46 basic characters
Dakuten and handakuten
Yōon
Reading loanwords
Foreign words get squeezed into Japanese syllable patterns, and once you know the rules, hundreds of words become readable without memorizing:

head: Katakana
Rōmaji
Origin
rows: coffee — ー lengthens the vowel before it
Jakarta — a consonant without a vowel gets a u
personal computer — two words cut and joined

blocks.title: Rules of thumb for loanwords
items: A consonant standing alone gets the vowel **u**: *milk* → ミルク *miruku*. Except after t and d, which get **o**: *hint* → ヒント *hinto*.
l always becomes **r**: *hotel* → ホテル *hoteru*.
The **ー** mark lengthens the vowel before it — in katakana only.
Your own name is written in katakana too. For example: John → ジョン, Emma → エマ, Michael → マイケル.

blocks.text: Particles are the skeleton of Japanese. Nouns don't change form the way they do in many European languages — what decides a word's role in the sentence is the little particle stuck after it, doing the job English gives to word order and prepositions. This table sums up every particle used in the ten units of this course.

head: Particle
Job
Example
Unit
rows: Marks the **topic** — “as for …”. ⚠️ Written は, read *wa*.
[わたしは|Watashi wa][がくせいです|gakusei desu]。
**Also / too**. Replaces は or を; doesn't attach to them.
[わたしも|Watashi mo][がくせいです|gakusei desu]。
**Ownership / origin / type.** The describing word comes first.
Marks the **object**. With verbs of motion: through, along.
**From** (time/place); at the end of a clause: **because**.
**Only**. Placed after the word it limits.
**Specific time**; **place of existence**; **destination**; the person you meet.
[さんじに|San-ji ni] · [きょうしつに|kyōshitsu ni]
Marks the **subject / new information**; what is liked/understood; mid-sentence: **but**.
[がっこうで|Gakkō de][べんきょうします|benkyō shimasu]。
[いいてんきですね|Ii tenki desu ne]。
**Tells** the listener something they don't know yet.
[それはわたしのですよ|Sore wa watashi no desu yo]。

blocks.title: The three pairs most often mixed up
items: **に vs で.** に = be in/at (Unit 5). で = do something in/at (Unit 6). きょうしつ**に**います / きょうしつ**で**べんきょうします.
**は vs が.** は = a topic already known. が = new information, or an emphasized subject. At A1, the rule “already known → は” rarely fails.
**と vs や.** と = a complete list (just these). や = a list of examples (this, that, and so on).

blocks.text: Every form used in this course, on one page. They all start from **the ます form** — the polite form that is the backbone of A1.

head: Form

Meaning
Unit
rows: [たべてもいいですか|tabete mo ii desu ka]
[たべてはいけません|tabete wa ikemasen]

head: Type
Present
Negative
Past
Past negative
rows: [しずかじゃありません|shizuka ja arimasen]
[しずかじゃありませんでした|shizuka ja arimasen deshita]
[がくせいじゃありません|gakusei ja arimasen]
[がくせいじゃありませんでした|gakusei ja arimasen deshita]

blocks.title: The two most stubborn mistakes
items: ⚠️ **たかいでした** — wrong. い-adjectives put themselves into the past: **たかかったです**.
⚠️ **わたしはも** — wrong. も replaces は; they don't stack: **わたしも**.
If you manage to avoid just these two, your Japanese will already sound far more mature than most beginners'.

blocks.text: Japanese doesn't count things with bare numbers. Each kind of object has its own counter word — like “three *sheets* of paper” or “two *loaves* of bread” in English, but compulsory and far more numerous. This table holds the most common ones.

head: Counter
Used for
Example
rows: Anything, 1–10. Your lifesaver when you forget the right counter.
Small, round objects: eggs, apples, stones
Long objects: pens, bottles, umbrellas, trees
Flat objects: paper, tickets, T-shirts, plates

blocks.title: Sound-change pattern
items: Sound changes almost always happen with the numbers **1, 3, 6, 8, 10** — and almost always in the same direction: the consonant doubles (っ) or turns into p/b.
1 → いっ～, 6 → ろっ～, 8 → はっ～, 10 → じゅっ～ · 3 → さん**b**～ (さんぼん, さんがい)
Once you see the pattern, new counters stop feeling like random memorization. You've already met the same pattern in hundreds (Unit 3), minutes (Unit 4), and floors (Unit 5).

blocks.text: Dates 1–31

blocks.title: Writing a full date
items: The order goes **from big to small**: year → month → date → day.
2026[ねん|nen] 8[がつ|gatsu] 21[にち|nichi] [きんようび|kin'yōbi] = Friday, August 21, 2026.
Japan also uses an imperial calendar: the **令和 (Reiwa)** era began in 2019, so 2026 = 令和8年. You'll see it on official forms, not in conversation.

blocks.text: Lengths of time
⚠️ **Mind the difference:** 3[じ|ji] = 3 o'clock (a point in time), 3[じかん|jikan] = for 3 hours (a length of time). One syllable separates an appointment from the length of a trip.

The hundred or so kanji below are the ones that appear most at A1, and they cover almost all the kanji tested in JLPT N5. This course deliberately doesn't force you to memorize them — the sentences are readable without them. But once your sentences flow, kanji stop being a burden and start being a shortcut: one character that gives you the meaning before you've even finished reading.

blocks.title: A way to learn kanji that won't wear you out
items: **Don't memorize readings as a list.** One kanji can have five readings, and the word it appears in decides which. Learn **the word**, not the character: 学生 (がくせい), not 学 = がく/まなぶ.
**Write by hand.** Copying ten times sticks far better than reading fifty times. Stroke order: left to right, top to bottom, horizontal before vertical.
**Spot the parts.** 語 (language) = 言 (word) + 五 + 口. 休 (rest) = 人 (person) + 木 (tree) — a person leaning against a tree. Kanji are rarely completely random.
**Five kanji a week is enough.** Twenty a week feels productive for three days, then stops altogether. The winner is the one who keeps going.

blocks.text: Numbers, time, and the calendar
People, places, and activities
Qualities, directions, and nature

**Irregular readings.** Some words use kanji with readings that can't be worked out from the individual characters: 今日 (きょう, today), 明日 (あした, tomorrow), 昨日 (きのう, yesterday), 一人 (ひとり, one person), 二十歳 (はたち, age 20), 大人 (おとな, adult). These are called *jukujikun*, and there are only a limited number — learn them as whole words.

All the vocabulary in this course, in English alphabetical order. The middle column shows the Japanese with its reading above it; the right-hand column repeats the reading in rōmaji for you to copy or look up in a dictionary.
If you've reached this page after working through the ten units — not just reading them — you've covered the whole of **Level A1 (CEFR)**, roughly equivalent to **JLPT N5**. Concretely, you can now:

items: Introduce yourself, and say where you're from, what you do, and who's in your family.
Ask and answer about prices, times, days, and places.
Describe your daily routine, and what happened yesterday.
Describe things, places, and people with adjectives.
Invite people, ask permission, and decline politely.
Read hiragana and katakana, and recognize about a hundred kanji.

blocks.text: And here's what you **can't** do yet — not to discourage you, but so you know exactly what the next level holds:

items: Speak in the plain form (dictionary form) used between friends — this course uses the polite ます form throughout.
Describe nouns with relative clauses: “the person I met yesterday”.
Compare: “A is more … than B”.
Express conditions: “if …, then …”.
The honorific language (敬語 keigo) used in the workplace.

blocks.text: The three most useful things to do now

blocks.title: 1. Don't stop reviewing
items: Languages fade because they aren't touched, not because they weren't studied enough. Reread one old dialogue every day — five minutes is enough to keep this whole course alive in your head.
If you stop for two weeks, don't start again from Unit 1. Read the Unit 10 dialogues, then work backward until you find what feels unfamiliar. It's usually less than you'd expect.

blocks.title: 2. Find real ears
items: This course prepares the material; what no book can replace is a conversation partner who responds — who stops when you make a mistake, repeats more slowly, laughs when your sentence comes out funny.
Linguo's private Japanese classes are designed for exactly that: your teacher matches the pace to the level you have right now. Ask at **linguo.id** for schedules and fees.
If you can't yet, at least listen to Japanese every day — dramas, anime with Japanese or no subtitles, NHK News Web Easy. Your ears need flight hours that reading can't make up for.

blocks.title: 3. If you're aiming for the JLPT
items: **N5** is exactly the level this course covers. The test is held twice a year (July and December) in many countries — check the official JLPT site for test centers near you.
What to add before you sign up: **listening** practice (the section that trips up candidates most) and reading practice **without furigana**.
Don't chase N5 if your goal is speaking. An N5 certificate is hardly used for anything official — its value lies in the deadline it sets for you.

blocks.text: Finally, one thing that's often forgotten: **you don't need to be perfect to be understood.** Japanese people are used to hearing broken Japanese and almost always try to meet you halfway. A sentence with the wrong particle that you actually say is far more useful than a perfect sentence that never comes out.
*[がんばってください|Ganbatte kudasai]。* See you at the next level.
